subsection: The mobility of modern economic activities and factors in their location

notes.b: Firms locate where total transport costs are lowest. This least-cost principle of industrial location was set out by Alfred Weber in 1909.
points: Bulk-reducing industries: the raw material loses weight in processing, so the plant locates near the raw material. Examples: alumina refining, dairy processing, fish processing, mining.
Bulk-gaining industries: the product gains weight or bulk in production, so the plant locates near the market. Examples: brewing, soft drinks bottling, bakeries.

Test for an exam location question: if the inputs lose weight in processing, the plant is pulled towards the raw material; if the finished product is heavier or bulkier, it is pulled towards the market.
Footloose industry: defined under the subsection Case study of a developed economy; the factors below explain where footloose activities choose to locate.
Branch plant: a factory or office owned by a company headquartered elsewhere, usually carrying out routine production.
Headquarters (HQ): the head office where a company's main decisions are made. Research and development (R&D): the work of designing new products and processes.
Greenfield site: undeveloped land on which a new plant is built. Brownfield site: land already built on, often a former industrial site that may need clearing before reuse.
Industrial estate or business park: a serviced area of land set aside for firms.
Cluster, or agglomeration: firms in the same or related industries grouped together, sharing skills, suppliers and research.
Backward linkages are links to a firm's suppliers; forward linkages are links to its customers.
Infrastructure: the transport, energy, water, communications and waste systems that firms depend on.

notes.b: A location factor is any condition that makes one place more suitable than another for an activity.
points: Raw materials: weight-losing raw materials pull processing towards their source or towards a port where they arrive.

Energy: industry once clustered on coalfields. National electricity grids freed most industry from this, but energy-hungry activities such as alumina refining and data centres still need large, reliable and affordable power.
Labour: the quantity, skills and education, cost, productivity and flexibility of the workforce.
High-technology and service firms seek graduates; standardised assembly seeks low wages.
Irish example for labour: the Intel plant at Leixlip and the Galway cluster, both described below.
Markets: the size and wealth of the market, and access to the EU single market. Bulk-gaining and perishable goods locate near the market; services locate near their customers.
Ports: deep water lets bulk carriers berth. Dublin Port is Ireland's busiest port. Port of Cork and Shannon Foynes Port are also major ports.
Rosslare Europort: direct ferry routes to France grew after Brexit (2021) to avoid the UK land bridge.
Whitegate, Cork Harbour: Ireland's only oil refinery, opened 1959.
Airports: air freight suits light, high-value, time-sensitive goods such as pharmaceuticals, medical devices and microchips.
Dublin Airport handled over 30 million passengers in 2023; its North Runway opened in 2022.

Freight modes: road offers door-to-door flexibility over short and medium distances; rail carries heavy loads on fixed routes; sea is the cheapest way to move bulk over long distances; air is the fastest but the most expensive.
Motorways, rail, broadband and fibre connect firms to markets and suppliers; for services, broadband and fibre matter most.
One environmental challenge of air transport is its CO2 emissions.
Capital: investment money comes from banks, shareholders, government grants and venture capital.
IDA Ireland was set up in 1949 and became an independent agency in 1969. It offers grants, serviced sites and advance factories to attract firms.
Corporation tax was 12.5% from 2003. Very large groups pay 15% from 2024.
Enterprise Ireland (1998) supports Irish-owned firms. Údarás na Gaeltachta (1980) supports enterprise in Gaeltacht areas.
Regional policy steers firms towards less-developed areas through grants and incentives.
Planning permission is needed before a site can be built on. EU state-aid rules limit the subsidies governments may give firms, while EU funds support regional development.
Trade agreements reduce the barriers that firms face when selling across borders.
Site: flat, well-drained land, large enough for expansion, at a cheap price.
Site: a water supply, and facilities for effluent and waste disposal.
Site: hazardous industry needs distance from homes.
Services: water, electricity, gas, broadband, waste treatment, housing and schools. Workers must be able to live near the plant.

notes.h: Agglomeration, inertia and quality of life
points: Agglomeration: firms in the same industry gather to share skilled workers, suppliers, research and universities.
Cork Harbour (pharmaceuticals) and Galway (medical technology) grew into clusters in this way.
Personal and historical factors: the choices of founders and the history of a site can decide a location.
Industrial inertia: an industry stays where it is after the original reason for locating there has gone.
Quality of life: attractive places to live help firms recruit skilled staff.

notes.b: Local opposition and environmental regulation can stop or delay a project. Corrib gas shows how long a delay can be.
points: Corrib gas was discovered in 1996. Its terminal is at Bellanaboy, Co. Mayo.
The Shell to Sea campaign opposed the project, and the Rossport Five were jailed in 2005.
Gas first flowed in December 2015, after a long delay caused by local opposition and changes to planning.
In the 19th century, raw materials and power were the main location factors.
In the 20th century, markets and labour became the main factors.
Today, footloose activities chase skills, tax, connectivity and quality of life.

notes.h: Aughinish Alumina, Co. Limerick: a raw-material and port location
notes.b: A bulk-reducing heavy industry located on a deep-water estuary, where imported raw material arrives by sea.
points: Aughinish Alumina opened in 1983 on Aughinish Island near Askeaton, Co. Limerick, on the south shore of the Shannon Estuary. It is Europe's largest alumina refinery.
Bulk-reducing: about two to three tonnes of bauxite make one tonne of alumina, so the refinery sits at the raw material's port.
Bauxite is imported by sea, mainly from Guinea and Brazil. The alumina (aluminium oxide) is shipped to aluminium smelters elsewhere; the refinery does not make aluminium.
Deep, sheltered water in the Shannon Estuary, Ireland's deepest natural sheltered water, allows large bulk carriers to berth.
The site is a flat island location away from towns.
Government support for heavy industry is a further factor in its siting.
Problems: bauxite residue, known as red mud, is stored in large disposal areas on site.
The company has been owned by the Russian company Rusal since 2007.

notes.h: Moneypoint and energy on the Shannon Estuary
points: Moneypoint power station, Co. Clare, is on the Shannon Estuary and imported coal by sea.
Coal burning at Moneypoint ended in 2025, so the estuary's energy role has changed.

notes.h: Intel, Leixlip, Co. Kildare: footloose high-technology manufacturing
notes.b: Intel is footloose in the sense that its products are not tied to a raw material or a market, so it chose Leixlip from many possible sites.
points: Intel's Leixlip plant opened in 1989. It is Ireland's largest private-sector investment, worth billions of euro.
Skilled graduates are available, with Maynooth University nearby.
IDA support and low corporation tax attracted the investment (see Capital, government and EU policy).
Access to the EU single market from an English-speaking base.
The plant lies beside the M4 motorway and close to Dublin Airport.
It occupies a large greenfield site with a supply of electricity and water.
Footloose does not mean likely to leave: the large fixed investment makes relocation unlikely.
Global job cuts announced in 2024 and 2025 affected Leixlip, showing that even a large plant depends on parent-company decisions.
Pfizer, Janssen (Johnson & Johnson) and Novartis are at Ringaskiddy; Eli Lilly is at Kinsale, Co. Cork.
The Port of Cork has deep-water berths at Ringaskiddy, which suits the import and export of pharmaceutical goods.
Large flat sites are zoned for industry, with water supply and waste facilities.
Skilled labour comes from University College Cork (UCC) and Munster Technological University (MTU). MTU was formed in 2021 from Cork IT and IT Tralee.
IDA support, tax and clustering reinforce the pattern.
Pharmaceuticals and chemicals are Ireland's largest goods exports.
Older heavy industry in the same harbour: Irish Steel at Haulbowline closed in 2001.
Boston Scientific opened in Galway in 1994. Medtronic, Parkmore, Galway followed.
The cluster draws on skilled engineers left by the closure of DEC's plant (see Location changes: Dell and DEC).
University of Galway research (renamed in 2022) supports the cluster, and a network of suppliers has grown around the firms.
Detail of Galway industry is in the peripheral Irish region subsection of Irish Regions — Core and Peripheral.

notes.h: Food processing near raw materials; brewing near the market
points: Kerry Group grew from the North Kerry Milk Products co-operative at Listowel, founded in 1972. Its headquarters are in Tralee, Co. Kerry.
Dairy processing is bulk-reducing: plants at Listowel and Tralee sit near the supply of milk.
Killybegs, Co. Donegal, is Ireland's largest fishing port.
Fish processing plants at Killybegs handle pelagic fish such as mackerel and herring, a bulk-reducing process that locates at the port.
Guinness at St James's Gate, Dublin, was founded in 1759 by Arthur Guinness on a 9,000-year lease.
Brewing is bulk-gaining because water is added to the product, so the brewery sits near its market.
Industrial inertia: Guinness still brews at St James's Gate today.

notes.h: Data centres: a modern location problem
points: Data centres used about 21% of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO).
EirGrid stated in 2022 that it would not connect new data centres in the Dublin region until about 2028, so the electricity grid now limits their location.
Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, Google and Meta operate data centres in Ireland.
Why Ireland: a cool, mild climate reduces cooling costs; fibre links to the USA and Europe; existing clusters of technology firms; tax.
Lower transport costs, through containerisation and air freight, let goods move cheaply over long distances.
Instant communications, through the internet, fibre and video calls, let firms manage plants at a distance.
Standardised production can be done by low-skilled workers, so the work can go anywhere with a cheap labour supply.
The removal of trade barriers, through the EU single market and the World Trade Organization, makes it easier to sell across borders from any member location.
Multinationals can compare countries and move capital quickly.
Investment brings rapid job creation, but jobs can leave just as quickly.
Branch plants are vulnerable because the decisions are made at a distant headquarters.
Countries compete for investment by offering tax and grants.
Expansion into new markets.
Getting inside a trade bloc, which gives tariff-free access to the EU.
Lower costs.
Access to skilled labour.
Following competitors into a cluster.
Tax planning.
Rationalisation: cutting surplus capacity after a fall in demand or a merger.
Relocation to lower-cost countries.
Outsourcing: contract manufacturers make the goods instead of the company's own plant.
Automation reduces the number of workers needed.
Mergers and takeovers, after which a parent firm may close a duplicate plant.
A product reaching the end of its life cycle.

notes.h: Upgrading as an alternative to closure
points: A plant can survive by moving up the value chain into more R&D, advanced products and services.
Intel's continuing investment at Leixlip is the example: Fab 34, opened in 2023, makes advanced chips using extreme ultraviolet lithography.
Dell opened in Limerick (Raheen) in 1990.
In January 2009 Dell announced that manufacturing would move to Łódź, Poland, with about 1,900 jobs lost in Limerick. It kept sales and service functions in Ireland.
Poland joined the EU on 1 May 2004, with nine other states, so its plants lay inside the enlarged EU with lower costs.
The full Dell case study is in The MNC and change subsection of The Global Economy — Multinationals and Globalisation.
DEC closed its Galway plant in 1993, and its skilled workforce later helped attract the medtech cluster.

notes.h: Product life cycle and changes in location
points: Introduction: the product is developed near headquarters and R&D, in a core region with highly skilled labour.
Growth: branch plants are opened in other developed countries near large markets; Ireland gained many.
Maturity: the standardised product is mass-produced in low-wage locations.
Decline: the plant closes or production is concentrated in the cheapest plant.

notes.h: Apple, Hollyhill, Cork: a location shift
points: Apple opened at Hollyhill, Cork, in 1980 and first made computers there.
As Apple's manufacturing moved to contract manufacturers in Asia, the Cork site shifted mainly to operations, support and services.
The Cork site is now Apple's European headquarters, with about 6,000 staff (2020s).

notes.h: What a host country can do
points: Attract firms early in new life cycles, for example in pharmaceuticals, medical technology and software.

Invest in education and research so that jobs are harder to move: Science Foundation Ireland, set up in 2000 and made a statutory body in 2003, funds research; it merged into Research Ireland in 2024.
Universities supply the graduates that keep high-technology firms in place.
Computing and the internet have made many services footloose, and Ireland became a European base for software and internet firms (see Case study of a developed economy).
Teleservices are services delivered at a distance by phone or internet, such as customer support, technical support and remote data processing.
Teleservices can locate anywhere with broadband, including peripheral areas.
Low-skilled teleservice work moves easily to cheaper countries or is automated.
The full MNC case of IT and teleservices is in The MNC and change subsection of The Global Economy — Multinationals and Globalisation.
E-commerce is buying and selling goods and services over the internet.
Warehouses and delivery depots locate near motorways and airports.
Pressure on town-centre shops, and bank branch closures, follow the growth of online trade.
Effects on an MNC's operations are in The MNC and change subsection of The Global Economy — Multinationals and Globalisation.
Remote and hybrid working grew after COVID-19, so some jobs can be done from home or a local hub rather than a city office.
National Broadband Plan: the contract was signed in 2019 with National Broadband Ireland to bring high-speed broadband to rural premises.
Connected Hubs: a national network of remote-working hubs launched in 2021.
Our Rural Future, rural development policy, 2021.
Broadband availability differs from region to region, and a region's coverage affects whether it can attract remote-working jobs.
Artificial intelligence and automation are future drivers of location and job change.
Automation can reduce the labour-cost advantage of low-wage locations, favouring places with skills and research.

notes.h: Method: two reasons for and one against
notes.b: Map and photograph questions ask why an activity might or might not locate at a point, using evidence from the map or photograph.
points: Name the factor, then give evidence from the map or photograph: a grid reference, or the photograph's location in accepted notation.
Explain why the factor matters to the activity.
Give three to five significant relevant points (SRPs) for each reason.
Use the same structure for a reason why the activity might not locate there.
Flat land and an edge-of-town site.
A national primary road or motorway, a railway, and a port or airport.
A town labour force and services: schools, hospital and housing.
Water and an existing industrial estate.
A pier, harbour or fishing port, on the coast.
Roads to markets.
Water and a labour force.
Low-lying land.
Coast, beach and scenery; lakes or mountains; antiquities.
A golf course, and water sports.
Nearby town services and road access.
Tourist information.

notes.h: Reasons why an activity might not locate at a site
points: Steep or high land.
A floodplain.
A protected or scenic area, where planning conflict is likely.
Poor roads, remoteness from labour, distance from services, and impact on residents.

notes.h: Worked example on an invented map
notes.b: The invented town of Ballyglas lies beside an invented N-road and river. All grid references in this example are illustrative.
points: Reason for locating: the flat land beside the N-road at illustrative grid reference M 142 335 gives room for a factory and its expansion.
Why it matters: a factory needs a large flat site, and the road gives access to markets.
Reason against: the river floodplain at illustrative grid reference M 140 333 would flood, so a plant there would be at risk.
Give advantages and disadvantages of the proposed factory site and of an alternative location, using accepted notation for the photograph.
Refer to features by their position in the photograph, such as foreground, background, left or right.

keyTerms.definition: A condition, such as raw materials, labour, markets, transport or government policy, that makes one place more suitable than another for an activity.
An industry free to choose its location because it is not tied to a particular raw material or market.
A factory or office owned by a company headquartered elsewhere, usually carrying out routine production.
Undeveloped land on which a new plant is built.
Land already built on, often a former industrial site that may need clearing before reuse.
A serviced area of land set aside for firms, often built by a public agency.
Firms in the same or related industries grouped together, sharing skills, suppliers and research.
A link from a firm to its suppliers.
A link from a firm to its customers.
The transport, energy, water, communications and waste systems that firms depend on.
An industry whose raw material loses weight in processing, so the plant locates near the raw material.
An industry whose product gains weight or bulk in production, so the plant locates near the market.
The principle, set out by Alfred Weber in 1909, that firms locate where total transport costs are lowest.
The tendency of an industry to stay in a place after the original reason for locating there has gone.
Cutting surplus capacity, often after a fall in demand or a merger.
Paying another firm, often a contract manufacturer, to make goods or provide services that the company used to make itself.
Services delivered at a distance by phone or internet, such as customer support and remote data processing.
Buying and selling goods and services over the internet.
A significant relevant point: one distinct, specific, examinable fact or explained point in an answer.

factCards.term: Aughinish Alumina: what it makes, where, when and two problems
factCards.definition: Europe's largest alumina refinery, opened 1983 on Aughinish Island near Askeaton, Co. Limerick, on the Shannon Estuary. It refines imported bauxite into alumina for smelters elsewhere (not aluminium). Problems: red mud stored on site; owned by Russia's Rusal since 2007.

factCards.term: Aughinish Alumina: why it is located on the Shannon Estuary
factCards.definition: Bulk-reducing: two to three tonnes of bauxite make one tonne of alumina, so it sits at the port where bauxite arrives from Guinea and Brazil; deep, sheltered water for large bulk carriers; a flat island site away from towns; energy supply; government support.

factCards.term: Intel, Leixlip: why a footloose firm chose this site
factCards.definition: Opened 1989. Skilled graduates, with Maynooth University nearby; IDA support and low corporation tax; access to the EU market from an English-speaking base; beside the M4 and close to Dublin Airport; a large greenfield site with electricity and water.

factCards.term: Intel, Leixlip: upgrading as an alternative to closure
factCards.definition: A plant survives by moving up the value chain: Fab 34 (2023) makes advanced chips using extreme ultraviolet lithography. The huge fixed investment makes moving unlikely, but Intel's global job cuts in 2024–2025 still affected Leixlip.

factCards.term: Cork Harbour pharmaceutical cluster: location factors
factCards.definition: Deep-water berths at Ringaskiddy; large flat sites zoned for industry, with water supply and waste facilities; graduates from UCC and Munster Technological University (2021); IDA support and tax; clustering of Pfizer, Janssen and Novartis.

factCards.term: Galway medical-technology cluster: how it grew
factCards.definition: DEC's Galway plant closed in 1993, leaving skilled engineers; Boston Scientific opened in 1994 and Medtronic followed at Parkmore; University of Galway research and a network of suppliers reinforced the cluster.

factCards.term: Kerry Group and Killybegs: industries located at the raw material
factCards.definition: Dairy processing is bulk-reducing: Kerry Group grew from the North Kerry Milk Products co-operative at Listowel (1972), near the milk supply, and is based in Tralee. Killybegs, the largest fishing port, processes pelagic fish such as mackerel and herring.

factCards.term: Guinness, St James's Gate: why brewing is located near the market
factCards.definition: Founded in 1759 by Arthur Guinness on a 9,000-year lease. Brewing is bulk-gaining because water is added, so the brewery sits near its Dublin market. It still brews there today, an example of industrial inertia.

factCards.term: Data centres in Ireland: location factors and the grid problem
factCards.definition: A cool, mild climate cuts cooling costs; fibre links to the USA and Europe; clusters of technology firms; tax. The problem is grid capacity: in 2022 EirGrid said it would not connect new Dublin data centres until about 2028, and in 2023 they used about 21% of metered electricity (CSO).

factCards.term: Corrib gas: how local opposition delayed a project
factCards.definition: Discovered in 1996, with a terminal at Bellanaboy, Co. Mayo. The Shell to Sea campaign opposed it and the Rossport Five were jailed in 2005. Opposition and planning changes meant gas did not flow until December 2015.

factCards.term: Freight transport modes: advantages, and one problem of air transport
factCards.definition: Road: door-to-door flexibility over short and medium distances. Rail: heavy loads on fixed routes. Sea: cheapest for bulk over long distances. Air: fastest, suiting light, high-value goods such as medicines and microchips, but costly and a source of CO2 emissions.

factCards.term: Government policy as a location factor in Ireland
factCards.definition: IDA Ireland (1949; independent 1969) offers grants, serviced sites and advance factories; corporation tax 12.5% from 2003, 15% for very large groups from 2024; Enterprise Ireland (1998); Údarás na Gaeltachta (1980); regional policy; planning; EU state-aid rules.

factCards.term: How the importance of location factors has changed over time
factCards.definition: 19th century: raw materials and power, so industry clustered on coalfields. 20th century: markets and labour, as electricity grids freed most industry. Today: footloose activities chase skills, tax, connectivity and quality of life.

factCards.term: Apple, Cork: a location shift through the product life cycle
factCards.definition: Apple opened at Hollyhill, Cork, in 1980 to make computers. As its manufacturing moved to contract manufacturers in Asia, the Cork site shifted mainly to operations, support and services; it is now Apple's European headquarters, with about 6,000 staff (2020s).

factCards.term: How a host country can hold on to mobile firms: two responses
factCards.definition: Attract firms early in new life cycles (pharmaceuticals, medical technology, software); invest in education and research so jobs are harder to move, e.g. Science Foundation Ireland (2000; merged into Research Ireland in 2024) and university graduates.

factCards.term: Broadband and the future location of jobs in Ireland
factCards.definition: Teleservices and remote work can locate anywhere with broadband, including peripheral areas, though low-skilled work moves abroad easily. National Broadband Plan contract 2019; Connected Hubs 2021; Our Rural Future 2021. Regional broadband gaps decide which areas gain.

factCards.term: E-commerce: three effects on where activities locate
factCards.definition: Warehouses and delivery depots locate near motorways and airports; town-centre shops come under pressure; bank branches close as business moves online.

factCards.term: OS map or photo: how to write each reason for locating an activity
factCards.definition: Name the factor; give the evidence (a grid reference on the map, or the photo location in accepted notation such as left background); explain why it matters to the activity. Develop each reason in three to five SRPs, and use the same structure for a reason against.

factCards.term: OS map: evidence that a site suits a factory or multinational
factCards.definition: Flat land on the edge of a town; a national primary road or motorway, railway, port or airport; a town labour force and services such as schools, a hospital and housing; a water supply; an existing industrial estate.

factCards.term: OS map: evidence that a site suits a fish processing plant
factCards.definition: A pier, harbour or fishing port on the coast; roads to markets; a water supply; a labour force in a nearby town; low-lying land.

factCards.term: OS map: evidence that a site suits a hotel
factCards.definition: Coast and beach, scenery, lakes or mountains; antiquities; a golf course and water sports; nearby town services; road access; tourist information.

factCards.term: OS map: reasons an activity might not locate at a site
factCards.definition: Steep or high land; a floodplain; a protected or scenic area where planning conflict is likely; poor roads; remoteness from labour and services; impact on nearby residents.

questions.prompt: Examine how labour and government policy have influenced the location of footloose industry in Ireland.
questions.model: Labour: Ireland has a young, English-speaking workforce with a high share of graduates, and universities such as Maynooth University, near Intel at Leixlip, supply skilled staff to high-technology plants. Skilled labour is concentrated in clusters: Cork Harbour's pharmaceutical firms draw on graduates from University College Cork and Munster Technological University, and Galway's medical-technology firms draw on engineers left by DEC when its plant closed in 1993 and on research at the University of Galway. Firms seeking skilled staff choose places where that staff already lives and studies, so labour pulls footloose industry towards existing clusters. Clusters also share suppliers and research, which lowers the cost of setting up a new plant nearby. Government policy: the IDA, set up in 1949 and made an independent agency in 1969, offers grants, serviced sites and advance factories to attract firms. Corporation tax of 12.5% from 2003 lowered the tax on profits of firms investing here, and very large groups pay 15% from 2024. Enterprise Ireland supports Irish-owned firms, and Údarás na Gaeltachta supports enterprise in Gaeltacht areas. Regional policy steers firms towards less-developed areas through grants and incentives. EU membership gives firms in Ireland access to the single market, and EU state-aid rules limit the subsidies governments may give, so the tax and grant policy works within those rules.

questions.prompt: Explain how raw materials and markets influence the location of manufacturing industry, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Raw materials: bulk-reducing industries locate near their raw material because processing makes the product lighter than the input. Aughinish Alumina, Co. Limerick, opened in 1983 on the south shore of the Shannon Estuary, where about two to three tonnes of bauxite make one tonne of alumina. Bauxite arrives by sea, mainly from Guinea and Brazil, so the refinery sits at a deep-water port that can berth large bulk carriers. Kerry Group's dairy processing at Listowel and Tralee, Co. Kerry, is bulk-reducing: milk loses bulk in processing, so plants sit near the supply of milk. Markets: bulk-gaining industries locate near their market because the product gains bulk in production. Guinness at St James's Gate, Dublin, is bulk-gaining because water is added to the product, so the brewery sits near its market. Irish-based multinationals use the EU single market as their market, which gives tariff-free access to a large group of consumers, so access to the market pulls manufacturing towards Ireland.

questions.prompt: Using evidence from an Ordnance Survey map, explain two reasons why a fish processing plant might locate in the area shown, and one reason why it might not.
questions.model: The invented Ballyglas map extract is used for illustration, and all grid references are illustrative. Reason 1, harbour and pier: a pier at illustrative grid reference M 142 335 provides a fishing port where boats land the catch. Fish is perishable, so a plant close to the landing point reduces the time between catch and processing. The flat, low-lying land beside the harbour, at illustrative grid reference M 141 334, gives room for processing buildings. The coastal location gives the plant direct access to the catch. Reason 2, roads and labour from the town: the invented N-road at illustrative grid reference M 146 339 gives a direct road link to markets for processed fish. Ballyglas, at illustrative grid reference M 144 338, supplies a labour force for the plant. Services in the town, such as schools and housing, keep workers living close to the plant. Reason against, a disadvantage: the narrow coastal road at illustrative grid reference M 140 331 is poor for heavy lorries carrying processed fish, and the plant would lie in a scenic coastal area where planning conflict is likely.
